summary: Proposes publishing directory schema inside the X.500 Directory itself. It presents a naming scheme for schema objects and a meta-schema for storing them. It is an experimental protocol.

eli5.summary: A directory has rules about what each entry looks like. This proposes keeping the rulebook inside the directory so everyone can read it.

questions: how to publish schema in x.500
what is a meta-schema in x.500
how to store schema in x.500 directory
how to retrieve unknown schema definitions
why distribute schema inside the directory
subtitle: Storing directory schema inside the X.500 Directory itself using a standard naming scheme.

tldr.problem: The X.500 Directory stores information, but the rules about what kind of information each entry can contain (the schema) had to be distributed by other means like FTP. This was a bottleneck as the directory grew.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 1804 proposes a naming scheme and meta-schema for storing schema information as regular entries in the X.500 Directory itself. A special subschema object at the root of each naming context holds schema objects for object classes, attribute types, attribute syntaxes, and matching rules.
tldr.outcome: Directory components can now fetch unknown schema directly from the directory using a standard algorithmic procedure, avoiding the need to distribute schema information separately.

facts.label: Schema storage location
facts.value: cn=subschema below the root of each naming context

facts.label: Schema lookup method
facts.value: Replace leaf RDN with oid=value, cn=subschema and search upward

today: RFC 1804 is an Experimental protocol published in June 1995. It proposed a practical solution to schema distribution before the 1993 X.500 standard provided built-in schema mechanisms. Today, X.500 implementations that support the 1993 standard typically use the standard schema distribution mechanisms rather than this approach.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
The X.500 Directory is a powerful system for storing and retrieving information about people, organizations, and other objects on the network. To interpret what is stored in the directory, all components must understand the schema: the rules that define what information each type of entry can contain.

Before this RFC, there was no standardized way to distribute schema information inside the directory. Administrators had to use external means like FTP to share schema definitions across the network. As the directory grew and served more applications, this became a severe constraint.
sections.eli5: When everyone uses the same phone book, they need to understand the same rules about what goes in each field. These rules need to be available to everyone who uses the book.

sections.title: Schema Management
sections.content:
Schema management involves four key tasks: storing schema information in the directory, retrieving it algorithmically, defining rules for modifying schema, and propagating schema changes. RFC 1804 focuses on storage and algorithmic retrieval, using existing X.500 mechanisms without requiring new protocols or functionality.

The proposal is simple: each naming context stores its own schema information below a standard location, so directory components can supply schema information for entries in that context without contacting other servers. This distributed approach avoids the need to maintain a central schema repository and prevents one slow server from blocking directory operations.
sections.eli5: Instead of one person keeping the rulebook, each neighborhood keeps its own copy of the rules that apply to that neighborhood. This way, you can always find the rules locally.

sections.title: Storage and Retrieval
sections.content:
Schema information is stored under a special subschema object named cn=subschema, located below the root entry of each naming context. The subschema entry is a regular X.500 entry that acts as a container for schema definitions. Children of the subschema entry represent schema object classes, attribute types, attribute syntaxes, and matching rules.

When a directory component encounters an unknown object type, it performs an algorithmic lookup: it replaces the leaf RDN (the specific object) with oid=<object-id>, cn=subschema and searches upward through the DIT (Directory Information Tree). This continues until it finds a matching schema entry at some level of the tree, retrieving the schema definition without requiring prior knowledge of where the schema is stored.
sections.eli5: When you see a phone number in an entry and do not know what it means, you look it up by name in the rulebook, which is kept in a standard place below your current location.

sections.title: The Meta-Schema
sections.content:
The RFC defines a meta-schema (a schema for schema) with four main object classes: subschema (the container), objectClass (stores definitions of object classes), attributeType (stores attribute definitions), and matchingRule (stores matching rule definitions).

Each schema entry is indexed by an object identifier (OID), so definitions are stored with names like oid=1.2.3, cn=subschema, .... Schema entries can include attributes like mandatoryAttributes, optionalAttributes, constraints on string and integer values, syntaxes, and whether the definition is obsolete. This allows the directory to store all necessary schema metadata in a structured, queryable form.
sections.eli5: The rulebook itself follows a standard format: a section for object types, a section for attributes, a section for how to match values. Each rule has a number and includes details like whether it is required or optional.

sections.title: Status and Considerations
sections.content:
RFC 1804 is an Experimental protocol. It was published in June 1995 and addresses a problem in X.500 directory deployment that existed before the 1993 X.500 standard revision, which added its own schema distribution mechanisms. This proposal provides an interim solution using existing 1988 X.500 mechanisms without requiring all components to upgrade to 1993 compliance.

The document explicitly states that security issues are not discussed. Schema distribution in a directory environment should include authentication of schema sources and access controls to prevent unauthorized schema modification. The proposal focuses on the technical mechanism; operational security policies are left to implementers.
sections.eli5: This is an experimental idea for X.500 directories, written in 1995. How you protect the rulebook so only the right people can change it is up to you.
